detail.abstract: The start and escalation of the 2026 Iran conflict have revived concerns about geopolitical oil and supply shocks, their macroeconomic consequences, and the appropriate monetary-policy response of the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve. Although extensive literature examines the historical effects of oil shocks, supply disruptions, and geopolitical risk on inflation, economic activity, and monetary policy, comparatively little research translates these historical experiences into forwardlooking assessments of ongoing geopolitical conflicts1 . This thesis addresses this gap by examining what historical geopolitical oil and supply shocks imply for a possible ECB and Fed policy response to the 2026 Iran conflict. The analysis tests the hypothesis that historical central-bank reaction patterns provide a reliable basis for deriving conditional policy implications for contemporary geopolitical shocks. A mixed-methods research design is employed, combining a historicalcomparative event study of major oil and supply shocks since 1973, extended Taylor rule regressions, eleven semi-structured interviews with chief economists, and forwardlooking scenario analysis. The results show that geopolitical oil and supply shocks consistently generate stagflationary pressures, while monetary-policy responses remain state-dependent. The extended Taylor rule regressions indicate that policy-rate persistence is the strongest determinant of interest-rate decisions in both jurisdictions. Beyond this, core inflation, liquefied natural gas prices, and geopolitical risk are identified as statistically significant drivers of ECB policy, whereas inflation expectations, unemployment and long-term Treasury yields emerge as significant determinants of Fed decisions. Applying these findings to the 2026 Iran conflict suggests that a temporary escalation of the conflict would permit for only a limited monetary policy reaction, whereas a prolonged disruption of energy markets would likely force central banks to engage in more drastic monetary tightening. By integrating historical evidence, econometric analysis, expert judgement, and market expectations within a single analytical framework, this thesis contributes a practical approach for assessing central-bank responses to future geopolitical supply shocks.

detail.abstract: Clavorà Braulin and Valletti (2016) show, in an insightful analysis, that a data broker selling customer information to two vertically differentiated retailers always prefers to sell it exclusively to one of them. The result relies on a Stackelberg standard for the asymmetric subgames in which one firm can price discriminate and the other cannot. We solve these subgames in mixed strategies under simultaneous price competition and show that the result is sensitive to this choice: on the symmetric locus of their model, for every admissible parameter vector, the broker's fee from selling to both firms strictly exceeds its fee from any exclusive sale. We then characterize the region of exclusivity exactly: it depends on a single universal constant, and the broker sells to both firms when the cost-quality ratio ∆ 𝑐 /∆ 𝑞 lies in the central 37.8% of its admissible range, whereas exclusivity remains optimal outside it. .

detail.abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence increase the amount of work people and organizations can complete while reducing the share of that work humans cognitively perform. This paper argues that the most consequential long-term effect is not job displacement or the erosion of individual skills, both of which are already well theorized, but the decoupling of work from experience. For most of organizational history, doing work produced the contextual understanding through which people learned to exercise judgment. That relationship is now breaking. I introduce experiential density, the amount of context-forming human participation contained in a unit of completed work, and Human Context Debt, the gap between the independently held contextual understanding a role requires and the understanding its holders actually form and retain under AI-mediated work. The paper makes three contributions. First, it distinguishes Human Context Debt from adjacent constructs (the ironies of automation, automation complacency, skill erosion, intellectual debt, cognitive debt and the apprenticeship problem) by shifting the object of analysis from skill to situated, social and institutional context, and from the individual task to the relationship between work and experience at every organizational level. Second, it identifies two mechanisms that prevent the time AI saves from being reinvested in context formation: a reinvestment fallacy, in which saved time is absorbed by interaction overhead, throughput expansion and visibility work, and synthetic context, in which even time devoted to reading and learning is increasingly spent on machine-generated material that carries representation without lived experience behind it. It also argues that low-density exposure is not additive: reviewing more AI-compressed material does not accumulate into understanding and can degrade it. Third, it reconceptualizes contextual stewardship as a capability that must be continuously reproduced rather than a residual human advantage, and derives eleven falsifiable propositions, a measurement approach and a four-condition experimental design. The central management challenge is not to preserve obsolete tasks but to preserve the developmental functions those tasks used to perform.

detail.abstract: Community-based educational spaces that work with marginalized youth remain written and examined in deficit or savior narratives. While many of the community-based educational spaces are doing asset-framed work (e.g., youth empowerment, civic engagement) with marginalized youth while still having to report on the ways they address negative outcomes (e.g., reduction in teen pregnancy, school expulsions). Building off Bergeson et al., (2025) asset-framed definition for these spaces (i.e., transformative community-based education programs [T-CBEPs], this qualitative study sought to understand Black female youths' experiences within a T-CBEP through Maton and Salem’s (1995) organizational empowerment framework. This qualitative study included a brief demographic questionnaire and two in-depth semi-structured interviews with six Black female participants. Semi-structured interviews allowed participants to answer specific questions and discuss other aspects of participation that they deemed important. The findings support and extend organizational empowerment's application at the individual and community levels. Emergent themes include: 1. Social support (i.e., bonding through macro adversity), 2. Leadership (i.e., individual investments), 3. Opportunity role structure (i.e., agents of change), and 4. Shared beliefs (i.e., attribution of individual success). Implications and suggestions regarding practice (e.g., school systems) and policy (e.g., federal level) impacting youth and youth programming are discussed.

detail.abstract: We characterize the compensation required to extend contingent late recovery from a low-cost manager to both private execution-cost types. Under explicit regional conditions and capped, monotone compliance wages, low-cost-only recovery leaves both types at the nonrecovery monitoring utility benchmark. Uniform recovery additionally requires high-type effort reimbursement, the conventional low-type rent increase, and a common utility increase pinned down by joint recovery, acquisition and early-adjustment incentives. In a matched record extension, verifiable actual acquisition removes that common uplift under separate sufficient conditions, even though the signal remains private; all three prescribed-policy compensation benchmarks are re-optimized. Additional resource-separation conditions yield an investor-policy ranking under the original records. On stated strict subregions, weak wage minima are strict-selection cost infima, not necessarily attained cheapest strict contracts. Acquisition certification is a hypothetical benchmark, not an established fund practice. Headroom determines feasibility, not optimal buffer size.

detail.abstract: Rubber Sheet Grading is an important quality assessment process which is traditionally performed manually, leading to inconsistency. Many deep learning approaches have been explored for grading rubber sheets automatically. Patch-based methods are widely used to learn local features from images. Although their integration in texture-based tasks remains challenging, this paper presents a comparative study between patch-based and full-image based deep learning approaches for rubber sheet grading. Experimental results show that the patch-based approach can capture fine-grained texture variations effectively, although classification performance varies across different quality grades. Patch-based techniques are particularly useful in scenarios with limited datasets, as patch extraction increases the number of training samples while preserving local textural information. Experimental results demonstrate that the patch-based VGG16+CBAM model achieves the highest image-level accuracy of 84.62%, compared with 64.10% for the full-image VGG16 approach, representing an improvement of 20.52 percentage points. The results highlight the potential of patch-based processing for capturing discriminative local texture information in rubber sheet grading, particularly when the available dataset is limited.

detail.abstract: A planner wishes to assign a scalar allocation to individuals with multidimensional types in a common values environment. She knows the mean and a lower bound on dispersion of types but not their distribution. Whenever the lower bound on dispersion is sufficiently small, offering the same allocation to all types maximizes worst-case expected welfare, even among random mechanisms. Menus allow individuals to choose their preferred options, but for every known mean there exists a distribution that misaligns willingness to pay with surplus, making any sorting strictly welfare decreasing. Applications to insurance and procurement illustrate the results.

detail.abstract: Published official statistics change after release. Advance estimates are replaced, monthly surveys are benchmarked to annual surveys and censuses, seasonal factors are re-estimated, indexes are rebased, and errors are corrected. Each change alters the data on which downstream models were trained and evaluated, yet real-time archives record that a series changed, not why. We introduce FedDrift, an open benchmark of vintage-labeled distribution shift in 17 monthly U.S. federal series from the Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. From 6,312 ALFRED real-time vintages (1949-2026), FedDrift derives 6,295 consecutive vintage pairs, of which 4,109 revise previously published values. Each such drift event records a revision footprint (depth, span, magnitude, direction, a censoring flag and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic on growth rates) and a cause label from a nine-class taxonomy. Labels are verified by the label owner at rule level (3,653 routine events under seven rules) and release level (456 events in 231 agency releases), against 361 registered agency documents with URL, publication date and SHA-256; 50 events are labeled unknown because no government source established their cause. FedDrift redistributes values only from public-domain agency files; the real-time layer ships as reconstruction code and hash-verified manifests. We define two tasks. On revision-cause attribution (T1), a depth-2 footprint tree reaches 0.870 accuracy but 0.372 macro-F1, and fails on causes absent from its training period. On real-time revision correction (T2), no simple correction beats the no-revision baseline (MAE 0.490 pp): every 95% bootstrap interval for the MAE difference includes zero.

detail.abstract: We solve the infinite horizon consumption and investment problem of an investor who is averse to falling short of past peak consumption, earns a constant labor income, and cannot borrow against that income. The solution is governed by two coupled free boundaries in the dual plane: a ratcheting boundary, where the standard of living is raised, and a borrowing boundary, where financial wealth is exhausted. We show that smooth recovery of wealth requires a mixed contact condition at the ratcheting boundary in addition to value matching. This condition places the ratcheting point strictly below the level dictated by instantaneous marginal utility and identifies it as the unique root of an explicit scalar equation. The borrowing boundary then solves a first order equation whose global solutions form a one parameter family with a common leading asymptote. Boundedness of a single homogeneous mode selects exactly one member of this family. We construct the doubly reflected state pathwise, including the corner where the two boundaries meet, and verify optimality over all progressively measurable admissible strategies without imposing a transversality condition. In the explicit solution the household keeps its standard fixed long after a myopic rule would raise it. For large standards, consumption at zero wealth converges to a fraction of income that does not depend on the degree of shortfall aversion. Under the baseline parameters it is hump shaped in the standard, and nonpledgeability costs a household without financial wealth about four fifths of its human wealth.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that executive cabinets should be deliberately built from members of different careers and political affiliations, a model it calls the Composite Cabinet. Most cabinets cluster around one profile: all one party, mostly business leaders, mostly career politicians, or mostly loyalists. That clustering narrows what a government can see, and it raises the risk of groupthink, blind spots, and brittle decisions under stress.
The paper first maps the space of cabinet compositions and shows it runs to millions of variations. It then draws on research in team diversity, organizational demography, and presidential decision-making, plus cases from Lincoln's cabinet to Switzerland's all-party Federal Council. It sets out eight benefits of a career-diverse cabinet and ten real drawbacks, including coordination costs, trust gaps, faultlines, and policy incoherence.
The core contribution is a hedging framework: twelve design mechanisms that keep the benefits of diversity while containing its costs. These include a shared cabinet charter, outsider-insider deputy pairing, structured dissent, and a measurable diversity floor. It then applies the model to United States politics and compares other democracies. A standalone segment examines tax avoidance by the very wealthy and why career-diverse leadership suits tax policy. The paper closes with an implementation model, metrics, and limits of the argument.

detail.abstract: On February 14, 2022, France enacted Law 2022-172, which introduces (by operation of law) a distinct regime for the sole proprietor (entrepreneur individuel). This regime establishes a separation between professional and personal assets and grants limited liability to the business assets. This division occurs automatically by operation of law, without requiring the creation of a separate legal entity. This legislative advancement affords the entrepreneur the benefit of limited liability for each business they own, thereby protecting their investments. The reform breaks with the principle of the unity of assets as a reflection of legal personality by allowing a single legal subject to maintain separate asset pools. This novel concept (the sole proprietor with limited liability) could serve as an alternative for protecting individual entrepreneurs and their businesses without the need to create a legal fiction. It could represent a de iure alternative for legal systems that currently lack these feature systems where, to secure autonomous assets and limited liability, one must incorporate as a company. Moreover, it could function as a mechanism that avoids unnecessary costs while facilitating the formalization of informal business activities.

detail.abstract: Language-model agents now act on payment services, mailboxes, files, and databases. Benchmarks report whether a task was completed, but task success does not show whether execution stayed governed when something went wrong. An agent may finish a refund and still have bypassed an approval, relied on stale evidence, or lost the record of why it acted. Interception, signed receipts, durable authorization state, and evidence-sufficiency scoring already exist, so this paper proposes a measurement study and no new enforcement mechanism. Agent-Gov-Bench asks one question: when execution breaks, does governance still hold? It measures governance continuity: whether authorization, approval validity, evidence lineage, provenance, and action consistency remain valid, or are correctly re-established, after an abnormal event, all classified on one execution trace against an independent external-effect ledger. The design injects faults across six scenario families and five action types, pairs each fault with a legitimate twin in which the correct behavior is to proceed, and compares four governance conditions: ungoverned, prompt-governed, permission-controlled, and runtime-governed. Metrics are reported as a vector with stated denominators and no composite score. A pilot of 160 runs precedes a frozen confirmatory protocol, and the final run count is set by the pilot and the power analysis, not fixed in advance. Passing the benchmark would not certify a system as safe; it would describe behavior under the injected faults only. No harness exists and no data have been collected.

detail.abstract:
Why do some societies adapt their institutions quickly after an external shock while others postpone change until a crisis forces it? This article advances one narrow claim: the more closed the channel through which political elites are selected, the longer a country postpones adaptive institutional reform after an external shock, and the more of the eventual change arrives in a single discontinuous step. The claim concerns the tempo of change, not the level of institutional quality, which earlier literature has treated extensively. 

The article specifies measures of closure, including clientelism as a proxy for clan loyalty and nepotism, measures of tempo, a duration model, and the conditions under which the claim would be rejected. It then uses three shocks, the Asian financial crisis of 1997, the global crisis of 2008 and the pandemic of 2020, and cases from Asia, Europe and Africa as illustrations, not as tests. Descriptive Archigos measures for the cases show that long leader tenure marks Indonesia and Malaysia, while short tenure in Thailand and Latvia reflects coalition instability, not openness. 

The same two shapes recur: delay followed by a break or a change of leader, and adaptation through an existing correction channel. The cases are consistent with the claim but cannot confirm it. Whether the regularity reflects a shared psychology of leadership, as proposed in earlier work (Nosalsky, 2026a, 2026e), is stated as a hypothesis for further research.

detail.abstract: Do regional value chains (RVCs) offer Africa a path to structural transformation that global value chains (GVCs) have not? We combine the EMERGING multi-region input-output tables for 2015 to 2023 with national accounts, employment, gravity, and trade-cost data to explore this question empirically. We develop a novel method to decompose RVC participation by sector and show that intra-African trade is highly manufacturing-oriented, suggesting potential gains from deeper RVC integration for structural change in Africa. Despite this, African RVCs remain small and concentrated within regional economic communities (RECs)-a pattern we term proto-regionalization. Forward RVC participation is associated with higher sector value-added and productivity, but primarily within mining and metals. Gravity estimates on intra-African trade and RVC flows show that agreements of the depth of existing RECs are associated with 66-84% more trade. However, documentary compliance costs and poor transport infrastructure continue to impede regional trade, and the AfCFTA has had no measurable effect by 2023. Extending REC-level agreements to all country-pairs (an effective AfCFTA) and upgrading trade procedures and roads to the level of Africa's best quartile would more than double intra-African trade in partial equilibrium. This would yield modest aggregate productivity gains of up to 15%, with considerable heterogeneity across countries. Crucially, the effects on between-sector labor productivity gains and employment shares, the core markers of structural change, remain positive but very small in magnitude.

detail.abstract: Public debate about AI and work centers on job loss, and policy frameworks, including one published by a leading AI lab, use the unemployment rate as their alarm. This paper argues that the main near-term harm is misallocation, which an aggregate gauge cannot see, and connects three documented failures to one missing funder. Drawing on published labor, tax, care-economics and learning research, it describes the three failures and proposes a single financing loop. First, AI is removing entry-level work, the rungs where judgment is formed. Early-career workers in the most exposed jobs show employment about 19% below trend while experienced workers do not. Second, the expert labor that trains AI models is paid hourly as contract work while the lasting value it creates is captured by platforms and labs. Third, the market underprices care work, the labor the country is shortest of and machines can least do. The paper argues all three share one cause, a missing funder. It proposes paying training labor as labor, through wages and residuals, and three steps aimed at the top. Close the tax code's tilt toward automation. Make data centers pay three times their power rate, with the difference covering household rates on the grid they use. Levy a charge on AI usage at the point of sale that exempts consumer plans and rises with volume. By rough estimate, a 10% to 25% charge on all current revenue would raise $20 billion to $50 billion a year, less after the exemption, enough to begin funding a care wage floor and paid apprenticeship years. None of it arrives as a gift. It points to the courts, regulators and voters already moving the money.

detail.abstract: Autonomous multi-agent AI systems increasingly plan, retrieve evidence, decide, and execute actions with limited human involvement, raising a governance question that is distinct from policy compliance: whether the evidence supporting a proposed action is itself sufficient to justify execution. This paper introduces evidence-bound runtime governance, a pre-execution control model in which proposed agent actions are gated not only by declarative policy but by an independent evidence-sufficiency check across five evidence states (Verified, Incomplete, Contradictory, Missing, Invalid). We present a four-condition ablation design (B0: no governance, B1: policy-only, B2: policy plus evidence validation, B3: full mechanism with riskbased escalation and continuous monitoring) intended to isolate the marginal contribution of evidence validation beyond policy enforcement alone, with the B1-versus-B2 comparison as the central analytic contrast. We specify a reproducible nine-category, multi-instance scenario corpus, a count-and-rate evaluation framework (policy enforcement rate, violation detection rate, false-positive/falsenegative rates, evidence compliance rate, escalation rate and precision, latency and overhead), and pre-registered hypotheses, statistical tests, and threats-to-validity for each research question. The contribution of this paper is architectural and experimental-design work: a governance mechanism, an ablation methodology, and a measurement framework for evaluating it. No experiments have yet been executed against this design; the paper accordingly reports no empirical results and makes no safety or performance claims beyond the proposed methodology itself.

detail.abstract: Safety evaluations usually ask whether an agent obeys a constraint. We ask an earlier systems question: does the execution path contain any decision locus that both receives the constraint and observes enough state to distinguish compliant from violating actions? We formalize this as a necessary availability × representability condition for selective enforcement and give a deterministic, modelindependent audit for testing it. detail.abstract: This study assessed the digital readiness of electric cooperatives (ECs) in the Philippines for the development and implementation of the National Electrification Administration (NEA) Learning Management System (LMS). It examined four dimensions of digital readiness: technology infrastructure, digital skills and competencies, digital culture and attitude, and organizational readiness. A mixed-method approach was used, combining quantitative survey data with qualitative responses from 240 employees representing 16 electric cooperatives. Respondents were grouped into three generations: Generation Z, Generation Y, and Generation X. The quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), Tukey's honestly significant difference (HSD) test, and the Kruskal–Wallis H test, while open-ended responses were analyzed thematically. The results showed an overall digital readiness mean of 4.33, interpreted as very high readiness. Organizational readiness obtained the highest mean score of 4.41, followed by digital culture and attitude (M = 4.39) and technology infrastructure (M = 4.33). Digital skills and competencies received the lowest mean score of 4.19, although this was still interpreted as high readiness. Statistical analysis revealed a significant difference in digital skills and competencies across age groups, with Generation Z respondents scoring significantly higher than Generation X respondents. Respondents generally viewed e-learning positively, particularly its flexibility and potential to support continuous professional development. However, internet instability and competing work responsibilities were identified as major challenges. A comprehensive repository of learning materials, mobile accessibility, and offline access were among the features most frequently identified as important. The findings suggest that the participating electric cooperatives are generally prepared to adopt the proposed LMS, but its successful implementation will require accessible learning resources, technical support, and opportunities to strengthen employees' digital skills. The study provides baseline information that NEA and the NEA-EC Training Institute can use to guide LMS development and implementation.

detail.abstract: The 15-minute city (FMC) has emerged as a central framework in sustainable urban planning, yet empirical evidence on how short-distance mobility is spatially structured within this framework remains limited. Existing studies have often assessed FMC through point-of-interest (POI) counts and catchment-based accessibility measures, while paying less attention to the built environment and sociodemographic conditions that shape actual localized travel behavior. Using 15-minute bikesharing trip records from the Seoul metropolitan area together with granular built environment, transportation infrastructure, and sociodemographic covariates, this study identifies neighborhood types associated with bikesharing-supported short-distance mobility. A two-step framework combining K-means clustering with complementary explanatory models reveals four spatially and functionally distinct clusters: a transit-oriented urban core, a flat-terrain urban core, a peripheral transit-deficient residential area, and a low-density suburban fringe. Across these clusters, membership is shaped primarily by street-network connectivity, multimodal transit accessibility, floor area ratio, and slope, whereas POI density and diversity do not emerge as leading predictors. This result suggests that the geography of 15-minute mobility is structured less by amenity counts alone than by the interaction of urban form, transport networks, and topography. The findings support geographically differentiated policy, including cycling-environment upgrades in urban cores, dock density and fare integration in transitdeficient peripheries, and land-use intensification in the suburban fringe. More broadly, the study shows that bikesharing can serve as an empirical lens through which the uneven geographies of short-distance accessibility are identified and interpreted.

detail.abstract: This paper is the third in a series following “Attribution Space: AMissing Concept in HSE Theory” and “The Structural Compressionof Attribution Space.” The first paper defined Attribution Space as the structural elasticity within which individuals can deflect responsibility for safety failures. The second paper demonstratedhow datafication and AI compress it through three pathways: granularization of information, elimination of temporal delays, andreduction of human judgment dependency. This paper argues that the compression of Attribution Space has an inherent limit. Three propositions are developed: (1) AttributionSpace never reaches zero; there exists an irreducible minimum; (2) there exists an equilibrium point and an optimal elasticity range; both under-compression and over-compression lead to system failure; (3) compression is a recursive process; data exposed ineach round becomes the input for the next round of compression. The paper proposes a spring model as a theoretical metaphor. The core formula is F = Kₛᵣ × ΔAS, where Kₛᵣ is the compressiondifficulty coefficient (not a threshold). The model contains four key nodes (P₀, P₁, P₂, P₃) and five compression zones (unmanaged, bonus, equilibrium, friction, overload). The paper validates the model through the Chernobyl nuclear disaster (1986) and the Fukushima nuclear disaster (2011), demonstrating that deviation from the optimal elasticity range leads to catastrophe. The paper further reveals the generative mechanism of system overload, the impossible triangle (compensation, standards, behavior), arguing that most modernsystems operate in an overloaded state: not incapable of running, but incapable of running healthily, liable to collapse at any moment. This paper does not argue for the elimination of Attribution Space. Rather, it posits that Attribution Space is not an enemy to be eliminated but a variable to be managed. The shift from“who” to“why” in HSE accountability has an optimal range, and identifyingthat range is the task of this paper.

detail.abstract: Affine-maximizer mechanisms provide structural incentive guarantees, but optimizing their agent weights and plan offsets requires solving a nonconvex mechanism-design problem. detail.abstract: Pressures on land, water, and food systems are intensifying under population growth, urbanisation, and climate variability, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This review synthesises recent advances across four interlinked domains: environmental management, soil-water modeling, agricultural sustainability, and precision agriculture. A structured narrative review of peer-reviewed articles, institutional reports, and preprints published between 1980 and 2026 was conducted, with emphasis on applied studies from the Guinea Savannah zone of Ghana and comparable settings. Evidence shows that Geographic Information System (GIS)-based multi-criteria decision analysis, especially the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), has become a standard tool for solid waste disposal site selection and groundwater recharge zoning. Remote sensing of multi-temporal imagery documents agro-ecological change around irrigation reservoirs, while microbial approaches, such as cyanobacterial extracellular polysaccharides, offer new routes to heavy metal sequestration. Soil water balance modeling and mechanistic soil-water-plant models provide the quantitative basis for improving fertilizer and irrigation use efficiency on smallholder farms. Precision agriculture, including sensing, robotics, and variable-rate input application, extends these gains to field and sub-field scales. The review identifies persistent gaps in data availability, model calibration, stakeholder weighting, and technology affordability, and proposes an integrated decision-support framework that couples spatial analysis, process-based modeling, and precision technologies to support resilient and sustainable land and water management.

detail.abstract: Lenders and listing platforms increasingly let AI systems judge homes from photographs that can also include the household, a cue that says nothing about the building. This study examines whether vision-language models assessing a property's condition respond to the race and facial expression of a household pictured alongside the listing images. Using a dataset of 18,000 observations, we evaluated real for-sale listings with five vision-language models under nine conditions: a no-portrait control and portraits of White, Asian American, Black/African American, and Hispanic/Latino families, each smiling or not smiling, with the property photographs held fixed. A household portrait raises the same property's overall rating and composite quality score for every group and modestly lowers the probability of a repair-risk flag. The benefit is unevenly distributed: relative to the White portrait, the Asian American and Black/African American portraits receive lower ratings, whereas the Hispanic/Latino portrait does not. A smile raises ratings for White and Asian American households, has no detectable effect for Hispanic/Latino households, and lowers ratings for Black/African American households. The favorable influence of an affective halo can thus coexist with racial disadvantage, and whether an expressive cue moderates that disadvantage depends on the household's perceived race. The within-property audit design gives platforms, lenders, and regulators a procedure for testing image-reading valuation systems for the disparities that nondiscrimination rules now require them to detect.

detail.abstract: Assigning maintenance work to an available technician can shorten dispatch delay while increasing diagnostic effort or repeat work if the assignment poorly matches the task. Conversely, reserving a specialist can improve execution but delay restoration and displace other critical work. This paper asks how task-specific skill matching should inform maintenance policy and assignment under financial, staffing, skill and scheduling constraints. A structured critical narrative review of verified scholarly literature is combined with symbolic decision analysis. No operational dataset, experiment, survey, simulation or estimated performance result is reported. The contribution is a conditional comparison separating initial restoration time from total attributable downtime over a defined repairquality observation horizon. An exact expectation identity incorporates the probability and conditional downtime burden of repeat intervention without assuming that every recurrence reflects technician error. It yields a specialistwaiting threshold and an associated cost comparison that includes the consequences of displacing other work. The synthesis compares corrective, preventive and condition-based maintenance and explains why authorisation, proficiency, diagnosis and independent verification require distinct treatment. Findings indicate that the quickest initial intervention need not minimise subsequent downtime, while an apparent specialist advantage may disappear when waiting and workforce opportunity costs are included. These findings are analytical propositions rather than measured causal effects. Practical application requires task-level competence evidence, complete timestamped work histories, explicit release criteria and locally justified uncertainty bounds. The paper provides a transparent screening method for assignment decisions, not a validated universal ranking of technicians or maintenance strategies.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the margins of marketing technology to the centre of how firms understand, reach and serve customers. This assignment examines three connected areas: how AI strengthens customer engagement through chatbots, recommendation engines and conversational interfaces; how it enables personalization at scale by using behavioural, transactional and contextual data; and how it improves marketing decision-making through prediction, optimisation and automation. The paper reviews the underlying technologies, presents illustrative company examples, weighs benefits against challenges, and discusses ethical and regulatory concerns such as privacy, algorithmic bias and transparency. It concludes that AI is most valuable when it augments human creativity and judgement rather than replacing them.

detail.abstract:
Background: Universities increasingly depend on digital medical records, patient portals, telemedicine and online scheduling to organise student health care. Yet installing digital technology does not establish that clinical and administrative outcomes have improved.
Objective: To synthesise empirical evidence on digital health administration in university-operated student health and counselling services, focusing on implementation, administrative processes, access, equity and service quality. 
Methods: A targeted, structured search of publicly discoverable academic literature and official publisher/identifier records was conducted in 2026. Studies published from 2019 to 2026 were considered if they examined actual campus health services or institutionally arranged digital healthcare for students. Twelve verified empirical reports were identified and critically mapped; two reports used the same 511-student Ghanaian survey and were not treated as independent datasets. A narrative thematic synthesis was used because designs and outcomes were heterogeneous. 
Results: Evidence linked Electronic Health Records (EHR) integration with better record visibility and service coordination; found variation in student telehealth availability between institutions; identified telehealth access benefits alongside privacy, workflow and clinician competency challenges; and documented student acceptance of online booking alongside infrastructural barriers. The evidence is mostly observational, qualitative or single-institutional; very few studies objectively quantify waiting-time reductions, costs, data breaches or academic effects. 
Conclusions: Digital administration should be evaluated as an institutional change process comprising governance, workflow integration, staff capacity, equity safeguards and accountable performance measurement. Strong causal claims about efficiency or student outcomes remain premature.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics are increasingly proposed as ways for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve decisions, raise productivity and strengthen competitiveness. Evidence from Ghana suggests, however, that most SMEs still rely on basic digital tools, and existing Ghana-focused studies concentrate mainly on what drives adoption or acceptance of a technology rather than on how analytics-supported decisions translate into performance. This paper develops a conceptual framework that treats managerial decision quality as the central mechanism linking AI-enabled analytical capability to productivity and sustainable growth. Integrating the technology-organisation-environment (TOE) framework with the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities and absorptive capacity, the framework proposes that (i) technological, organisational and environmental conditions shape AI-enabled analytical capability; (ii) capability improves performance largely through better, faster and more consistent decisions; and (iii) the strength of these links depends on data quality, employee analytical competence, management support and responsible implementation, including data governance and human oversight. Seven propositions and a set of testable hypotheses are derived, and boundary conditions specific to Ghana are identified, including infrastructure cost, record-keeping practices and the Data Protection Act, 2012. A quantitative-led, sequential mixed-methods design is outlined, with attention to power analysis, common method bias and reverse causality. The paper is conceptual: its propositions are not empirically established and require testing. It contributes a decision-centred, context-sensitive account of how AI may create value in SMEs, and an agenda for researchers, SME managers and policymakers.

detail.abstract: As generative AI becomes a visible participant in social media discourse, its influence extends beyond direct interactions to broader audiences. Moving beyond research on direct human-AI interaction or automated content governance, this study draws on the calculus of political participation framework to examine how public AI intervention affects the emotional extremity of subsequent discussion and whether such changes arise from changes in expression or participation decisions. Using approximately 342,000 news threads and over four million replies from X, a matched difference-in-differences design shows that public AI intervention significantly reduces the average emotional extremity of subsequent replies. This decline is accompanied by fewer high-extremity replies and no statistically detectable increase in low-extremity replies, a pattern consistent with changes in participation. The reduction is larger when the AI expresses a clear stance and occurs among both aligned and misaligned replies, with a larger decline among misaligned replies. Study 1 finds no statistically detectable effects on changes in participants’ positions or affective evaluations, or on intended-reply emotional extremity, but willingness-weighted emotional extremity is lower in the AI condition. This pattern is accompanied by lower willingness among participants who produced relatively high-extremity intended replies. Study 2 finds that lower reply willingness is associated with greater perceived risk and lower perceived influence when participants’ stances misalign with the AI, but with lower perceived influence and greater perceived redundancy when aligned. This study extends research on AI-mediated communication and offers guidance for governing public AI interventions while considering both emotional expression and viewpoint representation.

detail.abstract: Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) play an important role in international economic relations by establishing legal protections for foreign investors. However, these agreements also raise questions about the balance between investor protection and the regulatory sovereignty of states. This research examines the India-France Bilateral Investment Treaty, signed in 1997 and brought into force in 2000, to understand how it addresses this balance and what its evolution reveals about India's approach to international investment law and economic diplomacy. The study adopts a qualitative doctrinal research methodology based on an analysis of the treaty's provisions, relevant government policy documents, selected investment arbitration decisions and academic literature. India's 2015 Model Bilateral Investment Treaty is used as a comparative framework to examine developments in the country's investment treaty policy. The disputes in Cairn Energy plc and Cairn UK Holdings Limited v. Republic of India and White Industries Australia Limited v. Republic of India are also considered as comparative examples of broader issues concerning investor protection, state measures and investment dispute settlement. These cases arose under different treaties and are therefore not treated as direct interpretations of the India-France BIT. The research examines the legal protections established by the India-France BIT, the potential tensions between investor rights and state regulatory authority, and the wider significance of India's evolving investment treaty approach. It considers how treaty design and dispute settlement mechanisms relate to the management of international economic relations. The study aims to contribute to a clearer understanding of the relationship between investment protection, economic sovereignty and economic diplomacy in the context of India-France relations.

detail.abstract: Many groups keep a recognizable emotional character for years even as their members are replaced. Across 1,004 Reddit communities from 2007 to 2025, covering 431.6 million comments by 22.2 million people, we find that the emotional tone of a community barely moves from year to year, and holds largely over a decade, even though 75% of the members of a community change each year. If the people keep turning over, what holds the tone in place? To answer this question, we examine 4.9 million cases in which someone already active elsewhere joins a new community, comparing how they wrote before with how they write once inside. This separates selection (attracting people who already fit) from conversion (reshaping whoever arrives). We find that selection barely registers. Newcomers do not choose communities by tone; they take on the tone of the place they enter. About 85% of the gap between a newcomer’s tone and the community’s closes at their very first comment, before a single reply or vote. Votes, departures, and heavier moderation change little. A steady-state model confirms that this conversion is what keeps a community’s tone stable: without it, only the part of tone set by the community’s topic would last, and the rest would fade within a few years. Our findings suggest that the emotional character of a community is a property of the setting rather than of its members, and replacing individuals is unlikely to change it while newcomers keep converting.

detail.abstract: Multiplier analysis normally takes it for granted that tax revenue returns to the circuit as effective demand, in full and within the period. We argue that this is not so when a single central layer of government is asked to allocate goods that are local, heterogeneous and dependent on dispersed information, and we call the resulting shortfall Sovereign Lag. The remedy examined here is a second, civic layer of fiscal authority. Under a Citizen's Executive Right (CER), a constitutionally fixed share of revenue is credited to non-transferable personal accounts, which citizens assign to certified non-profit providers, while redistribution, stabilisation and debt management remain with the macro state. A lapsing rule with a two-sided demurrage and a labour-share condition on providers connect the two layers. A stock-flow consistent matrix checks the accounting. In a Goodwin growth-cycle model extended with the civic injection the equilibrium becomes locally stable and the wage share rises, but the employment rate fixed by wage formation is unaffected. In a Kaleckian two-class multiplier the civic channel adds to demand only if providers are more labour-intensive than the market sector. Open-economy leakages and the politics of entrenchment are discussed more briefly.

detail.abstract: What evidence remains after a trading rule is rejected? We audit one team's research archive of 283 records. "Registered" means that the candidates' registration records were retained; the classification of rejections was frozen retrospectively, on 15 October 2026. Of 210 main-analysis rejections, 52 come from designs with no common economic threshold. Of the other 158, the frozen classification finds 23 nominal exclusions of a specified positive advantage, 52 non-exclusions and 83 rules whose records are missing or incompatible. A separate re-examination layer re-estimates the 23 exclusions from archived training series with dependence-robust standard errors: 22 are retained (the upper bound stays below the threshold, which does not validate the rule's absence of value) and one, Q223, is overturned. Under Holm or Romano–Wolf familywise correction, 14–15 of these exclusions remain. The three evidence layers are not interchangeable: re-examination adds evidence without rewriting the frozen classification, and simulations are synthetic diagnostics, not estimates for this archive. The paper offers an audit framework and one case, a single team's archive with no denominator for ideas discarded before registration, not a claim about research in general. Stopping conditions and information states are reported as co-occurrence patterns, not causes, and the results do not identify historical missed discoveries. AI disclosure: research execution (coding, computation, record extraction and audit, numerical reconciliation) and drafting were carried out with Claude (Anthropic) and GPT (OpenAI) under the author's direction; the author set the research programme, authorized all data access, and is responsible for the content.

detail.abstract: Climate Adaptation finance is a critical but severely underfunded aspect of India's climate strategy. Unlike mitigation with clear benchmarks such as renewable energy capacity or emission reductions, adaptation projects address more complex, context-specific vulnerabilities, spanning areas like climate-resilient infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and community-level resilience building. However, these projects often face barriers to funding and implementation due to their "public goods" nature and lack of business models to attract private investors. detail.abstract:
This paper looks closely at the greenwashing methods implemented in fast fashion and the luxury industry through the framework created by TerraChoice in 2007, The "Six Sins of Greenwashing": A Study of Environmental Claims in North American Consumer Markets.

This study aims to examine real examples across each of the six categories, namely Sin of the Hidden Trade Off, Sin of No Proof, Sin of Vagueness, Sin of Irrelevance, Sin of Fibbing, and Sin of the Lesser of Two Evils, to present a comparative analysis between both sectors.

The research relies on secondary data, primarily sustainability and climate reports from various brands, to check their claims against measurable data and recognized third party sources. Legal proceedings against false claims have also been studied. This is done to recognize patterns of greenwashing and understand how different levels of production lead each industry to mislead consumers in different ways.

By examining relevant examples under each category, the findings clearly indicate a distinct pattern. While the fast fashion industry mainly commits the Hidden Trade Off and Vagueness to promote false claims, luxury brands generally show a lack of proof regarding how sustainable their materials actually are. This difference stems directly from the contrasting production volumes and quality standards of each industry.

Finally, the paper addresses key limitations, including silent brands that make no environmental claims and geographic disparities where sustainability is only practiced in domestic markets, or countries of origin, while manufacturing hubs and other global franchises are overlooked.

detail.abstract: We study a channel of quantitative easing (QE) that operates through the renegotiation of existing bank loans. Matching syndicated-loan amendment histories to bank balance sheets, we find that larger purchases of agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) are associated with more renegotiation at exposed banks, with the increase concentrated in amendments that favor lenders. Relative to other loans of the same firm in the same quarter, a doubling of quarterly purchases is associated with committed amounts 2.5 percent lower, spreads 10.6 basis points higher, and maturities 3.1 percent shorter on exposed banks’ amendments. The response is present among borrowers in covenant compliance and no stronger among those in violation, distinguishing it from renegotiation driven by creditor control rights in technical default. It is concentrated among well-capitalized, well-provisioned, and profitable banks and among less profitable, lower-valuation, but not highly leveraged borrowers, consistent with a bargaining channel in which financially strong lenders extract larger concessions from borrowers with weaker outside options. A shift-share design indicates that a ten-percentage-point increase in lender-favorable renegotiation lowers firms’ annual investment rate by 6 percent of its mean. QE thus tightened existing corporate credit for borrowers of exposed banks, potentially offsetting part of its expansionary effects on new lending.

detail.abstract:
Better forecasts do not necessarily produce a better global equity portfolio. The question is whether those signals improve the final portfolio once benchmark-relative risk, overlapping holdings, trading, and costs are taken into account. This paper examines a global equity ETF portfolio that combines machine-learning selection, benchmark-aware regional allocation, and a small allocation across themes, sectors, and styles. The components are evaluated together against the iShares MSCI ACWI ETF (ACWI).

The common daily evaluation covers 31 January 2019 through 31 August 2026. In this reconstructed research history, the portfolio compounded at 18.9% annually versus 13.8% for ACWI, with 6.15% tracking error, a 0.819 information ratio, and a maximum relative drawdown of 8.10%. The advantage was uneven: the portfolio lagged ACWI in 2022, rolling active returns turned negative in some periods, and primary selection alone had a better recent trade-off between active return and tracking error than the complete portfolio.

Longer component histories include additional market environments but are not a longer backtest of the integrated portfolio. Because the model combination was selected during research, the evidence does not establish an optimal mix. The relevant test is what each component contributes after the portfolios are combined.

detail.abstract: Farmer identity is receiving growing attention as a concept for understanding heterogeneity in farmers' agri-environmental decision-making and behavior. Drawing on a systematic review of quantitative studies, we critically assess the current state of research on farmer identity and how it relates to agri-environmental outcome variables. While conservationist identity has largely positive associations with agri-environmental outcomes, the results for productivist identity are mixed, showing both negative, positive, and non-significant associations. This variation seems to partly reflect differences between agri-environmental measures in the extent to which they align with productivist identities and farming objectives. Our review further reveals substantial heterogeneity in how farmer identities are measured and labeled across studies. Finally, we discuss the limited explanatory depth of studies reporting associations between farmer identity and agri-environmental outcomes. We outline directions for future research to improve our understanding of when, how, and under what conditions farmer identities shape agri-environmental decision-making and behavior, in order to strengthen the relevance of this literature for supporting agricultural change.

detail.abstract: In the dual institutional context of China, which fosters innovation-led growth while implementing reforms in shareholder-focused capital markets, this research investigates the impact of managerial myopia on corporate investment in innovation. It particularly delves into the mechanisms (such as dividend payout and cash flow) and situational factors (including growth prospects and media scrutiny) by which short-term managerial choices influence the distribution of resources for innovation. Utilizing panel data from Chinese A-share listed firms spanning from 2012 to 2024, we apply instrumental variable regression, lagged analysis, and bootstrap mediation techniques to explore the impact of managerial myopia on the allocation of resources between innovation and distributions to shareholders. T The study investigates how dividend payout ratio and operating cash flow orientation mediate relationships, in addition to exploring the moderating influences of growth opportunities and media attention, all while considering endogeneity and other potential explanations. The results indicate that (1) a short-sighted managerial approach considerably diminishes corporate investments in innovation; (2) such managerial short-sightedness reallocates financial resources from innovation investments by means of an increased dividend payout ratio and an enhanced emphasis on operating cash flow; (3) opportunities for growth amplify the detrimental impact of a higher dividend payout ratio on corporate innovation investment, while media coverage mitigates the negative influence of managerial myopia by enhancing external information oversight and reputational pressures. This study advances understanding of how managerial time horizons, resource allocation, and innovation interact in emerging capital markets. The findings highlight the tension between short-term shareholder-return policies and long-term innovation outcomes, offering evidence-based insights for policymakers and corporate leaders on balancing shareholder demands with sustainable innovation.

detail.abstract: Time spent studying has fallen dramatically in higher education (Babcock and Marks, 2011). Given high opportunity costs of college and low on-time graduation rates,1 policymakers have sought to fill this perceived free time with more credit hours to keep students on-track and engaged (Attewell et al., 2012). This assumes students will allocate the additional time required by added courses. Instead, they may substitute leisure inelastically to preserve current utility from activities like exercise at the cost of worse grades, offsetting future labor market benefits of academic success (Freier et al., 2015; Hansen et al., 2024; Jones and Jackson, 1990; Khoo and Ost, 2018). In the extreme, broad policies such as tying financial aid to enrollment minimums (Scott-Clayton, 2011) may dissuade some from attending university at all. Despite its importance, leisure time data is rarely collected and existing work has focused almost exclusively on academic outcomes. We address this gap by estimating the causal effect of larger course loads on leisure time directly. We then examine impacts on not only course grades but also physical fitness and success in extracurricular activities to provide insight into how course loads affect student well-being in multiple domains rather than academics alone.

detail.abstract: Rising statutory retirement ages have renewed concerns that workers in physically and psychologically demanding occupations may be unable to extend their working lives due to health deterioration. This paper provides the first decomposition of the effect of occupational job strain on early retirement, separating the health-mediated channel - the central empirical justification for occupation-specific early retirement schemes - from financial and institutional channels. Linking survey data from SHARE and SOEP with German administrative pension records, I construct lifetime occupational strain measures and estimate a mediation framework that accounts for exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounders. The total effect is small and insignificant: a one-standard-deviation increase in lifetime strain raises the probability of early retirement by only 1.5-2.4 percentage points. The health-mediated indirect effect is negligible - I can rule out with 95% confidence that it exceeds 0.75 percentage points per standard deviation, and it falls to essentially zero once disability pension recipients are excluded, indicating that Germany’s disability insurance already absorbs most health-driven exits. Financial and institutional channels dominate instead: high-strain workers accumulate fewer pension points and fewer work years, reducing both eligibility and the financial capacity for early retirement.

detail.abstract: Spare-parts pooling can reduce duplicated inventory across manufacturing sites, yet an available shared component does not necessarily restore production promptly. Transport, competing requests, qualified labour and shutdown access can determine whether inventory sharing improves equipment availability. This paper asks under what conditions pooling should accompany corrective, preventive or condition-based maintenance when financial, staffing, skill and scheduling resources are constrained. A structured critical review of verified scholarly sources is combined with an original analytical comparison of restoration times. The study uses no operational dataset, simulation or estimated performance results. Its contribution is a conditional decision test that distinguishes earlier part arrival from earlier restoration, using the maximum of part, crew and access readiness rather than adding overlapping delays. For otherwise identical interventions, an exact positive-part identity identifies when a change in part arrival affects downtime. A corresponding expected-cost comparison separates inventory savings from transport, administration and production-loss consequences. The analysis shows why partial pooling, local protection for time-critical components and advance reservation for planned interventions deserve consideration alongside complete sharing. It also identifies repair capacity and correlated requests as constraints that inventory aggregation alone cannot resolve. The findings provide a transparent basis for policy screening and local validation; they do not establish universally optimal stock levels or quantified savings. Manufacturing implementation requires compatible components, traceable transactions and explicit allocation rules aligned with site-level service commitments.

detail.abstract: This article examines whether local exposure to the 1918 influenza pandemic affected wage inequality across U.S. counties by 1940. We leverage the role of World War I military camps in diffusing influenza to civilian populations and construct a county-level exposure measure that combines proximity to the nearest camp with camp-level outbreak intensity, proxied by soldiers’ hospital admissions during the second wave. Combining historical military records with complete-count 1940 U.S. Census data, we find that more exposed counties displayed higher wage inequality among male workers in 1940. We then use linked 1910–1940 Census records to examine the mechanism behind this aggregate pattern. The individual-level evidence suggests that the adverse wage effects of pandemic exposure were concentrated among men who were children or adolescents during the pandemic and came from disadvantaged family backgrounds. These results indicate that the 1918 influenza pandemic widened wage inequality by worsening the long-run labor-market outcomes of initially disadvantaged cohorts.

detail.abstract: Testosterone has been linked to social and economic outcomes in studies dating back to the 1970s (Dabbs, 1992; Kreuz and Rose, 1972; Mazur and Lamb, 1980). Testosterone affects physical development (e.g., the development of male characteristics in utero or during puberty, muscle mass), but also influences behavioural responses (Phoenix et al., 1959). For example, in humans, testosterone has been linked to status-enhancing behaviour (Dreher et al., 2016), such as aggressiveness (Carré and McCormick, 2008), risk-taking (Apicella et al., 2008; Coates and Herbert, 2008) but also prosocial behaviour (Dreher et al., 2016; Schaal et al., 1996). This latter association between testosterone and behaviour, in particular, inspired a strand of the literature examining the role of testosterone for labour market outcomes (Dabbs, 1992; Dabbs Jr. et al., 1990). For example, studies report that higher testosterone is associated with higher rates of self-employment (Greene et al., 2014; Nicolaou et al., 2017), careers in “risky” occupations such as finance (Nye and Orel, 2015; Sapienza et al., 2009), and higher earnings (Gielen et al., 2016; Hughes and Kumari, 2019; Nye et al., 2017).

detail.abstract: We study China's commercial system reform in 2014, which greatly simplified the requirements for firm registration and market entry. Using a continuous difference-indifferences design, we exploit cross-city variation in baseline rural population share across 280 Chinese prefecture-level cities to identify heterogeneous reform effects on firm entry intensity in labor-intensive industries. The research indicates that the reform had stronger effects on firm entry intensity in labor-intensive industries in cities with higher baseline rural population share, highlighting the role of local labor-market structures in shaping the response to deregulation. Mechanism analysis points to a primary labor-reallocation channel associated with per capita rural disposable income: the reform effect is stronger where the opportunity cost of reallocating rural labor is lower. A complementary market access channel further amplifies the response in cities with better access to surrounding markets. These findings show that reducing entry barriers alone does not determine the magnitude of deregulation effects; the local labor and market environments in which reforms operate are also important.

detail.abstract: Do higher wages raise labor productivity? This paper studies that question using a structural production framework motivated by efficiency-wage theory. Higher wages may increase effective labor through worker effort, selection, retention, and related mechanisms. At the same time, wages are endogenous because more productive firms may also choose to pay more. We develop a model in which firms jointly choose employment, materials, and wages, while effective labor depends on employment, a wage-response function, and labor-augmenting productivity. This allows us to separate the wageresponse channel from Hicks-neutral and labor-augmenting productivity shocks commonly modeled in the IO productivity literature. We apply the model to establishment-level panel data from Colombian manufacturing over 2010–2019. The estimated wage elasticity of effective labor is about 0.27, indicating a positive but modest labor-efficiency response to higher wages. This estimate is well below the unit elasticity implied by the frictionless efficiency-wage benchmark. The results provide evidence that wages affect production through the labor-efficiency margin. More broadly, the findings connect efficiencywage theory to structural production-function estimation and show that wage-setting may matter for firm productivity in developing-country manufacturing.

detail.abstract: Accurate state of charge (SOC) estimation is essential for battery management system (BMS) energy management and safety control. This paper develops an extended patch bidirectional long short-term memory (XPatch-BiLSTM) model with trend-residual dual streams for SOC estimation using real-world vehicle data. Multivariate BMS sequences are decomposed into trend and residual components, which are modeled by BiLSTM and XPatch branches, respectively, to capture global state evolution and local dynamic variations. Spearman correlation, mutual information, and LightGBM-based permutation importance are integrated for feature construction. On six primary operating segments, the model achieves mean absolute error (MAE) values of 0.2869%–0.3482% and root mean square error (RMSE) values of 0.3522%–0.4328%. Compared with seven baselines, XPatch-BiLSTM achieves the lowest mean MAE, RMSE, and maximum error (ME) of 0.3176%, 0.3930%, and 1.2735%. Extended evaluation on six additional sequences from three vehicles yields ME values below 2% for all sequences. Parameter sensitivity, ablation, and noise analyses further support the adopted model configuration and estimation stability.

detail.abstract: This systematic literature review examined the relationship between tax knowledge and tax compliance, demographic differences, and their implications for developing a Taxpayer Support Toolkit, particularly for sole proprietorship taxpayers in the Philippines. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) framework, the review employed systematic search, screening, quality appraisal, and thematic synthesis of relevant scholarly literature. The review focused on tax knowledge in terms of awareness of tax laws, understanding of tax rates, and familiarity with tax obligations, alongside tax compliance concerning timely filing, accuracy of tax declarations, and payment of correct tax amounts. Findings consistently indicated that greater tax knowledge was associated with improved voluntary compliance, although regulatory complexities, procedural misunderstandings, and limited access to practical tax education remained persistent challenges. Demographic characteristics, including age, sex, educational attainment, monthly income, and engagement of accountants or third-party tax services, were also identified as potential sources of variation in tax knowledge and compliance behavior. Despite extensive research on these variables, limited integrated evidence specifically addressed their relationships and demographic differences among Philippine sole proprietorship taxpayers. The review concludes that targeted, accessible, and practical taxpayer education is essential to addressing knowledge gaps and compliance difficulties. These findings provide a conceptual basis for developing a Taxpayer Support Toolkit responsive to taxpayers' diverse informational and procedural needs.

detail.abstract: Stock price movements following corporate earnings announcements are influenced by both broad market conditions and company-specific information, making it difficult to determine the underlying source of an observed price change. Traditional financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) provide an interpretable framework for estimating systematic market exposure, but their linear formulation limits their ability to capture complex and nonlinear relationships in financial data [1], [2]. Recent advances in machine learning have demonstrated the ability of tree-based models to learn nonlinear interactions among financial predictors [3], while Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) enable feature-level interpretation of complex model outputs [4]. Furthermore, post-earnings announcement drift demonstrates that stock prices may continue to respond to earnings-related information beyond the initial announcement period [5]. This paper presents Stock DNA AI, an explainable artificial intelligence framework for decomposing postearnings stock movements of National Stock Exchange (NSE)-listed equities into systematic marketdriven and idiosyncratic company-specific components. The proposed framework employs an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)-based CAPM layer to estimate the stock's market-driven return relative to the NIFTY 50 index and an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model to capture nonlinear relationships among financial, market, and technical indicators. SHAP TreeExplainer is subsequently employed to identify the contribution of individual features to model predictions. The resulting information is integrated into an interactive React-based dashboard through a FastAPI backend, providing prediction, market-versuscompany attribution, and feature-level explanations within a unified interface. Experimental evaluation conducted on NIFTY 50 stocks achieved a 67.8% directional prediction accuracy. The framework therefore demonstrates the feasibility of combining established financial theory, machine learning, and explainability.

detail.abstract: Every year, millions of young Indians finish school or college and walk straight into a wall. They have the degree their families worked and saved for, and no job to put it to use. This paper asks a deceptively simple question — what does that do to an economy? — and answers it from where Anvika and this study sit: India, the country with the largest population of young people on Earth. Three ideas run through the paper. The first is that youth unemployment in India is not just personal bad luck; it is a national balance-sheet problem, draining output, tax and spending while the bill for inactivity quietly grows. The second is India’s strange signature: here, the more education a young person has, the harder it can be to find work — graduate unemployment ran near 29% in 2022, roughly nine times the rate for those who never learned to read. The third is the newest twist. Artificial intelligence is learning to do exactly the simple, first-year tasks — basic coding, testing, data work, drafting — that India’s vast IT-services industry once used to absorb hundreds of thousands of freshers. The first rung of the ladder is fraying at the very moment India most needs it to hold. The paper examines the most vulnerable groups affected by the crisis (including the educated youth and, above all, young women), its causes, the price tag, what other countries have done right, and what India is doing about it using data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey conducted by the Government of India, the report from the World Employment Report 2024 produced by the India Employment Report, and data from the International Labour Organization (ILO), World Bank, and the World Economic Forum. detail.abstract:
Sustainable consumption behaviour (SCB) research has grown enormously over the past three decades,
yet the dominant theoretical frameworks (the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Value-Belief-Norm theory,
and related voluntary-choice models) were developed almost exclusively in high-income, institutionally
stable contexts. This study argues that these frameworks embed an implicit but consequential assump-
tion that the institutional preconditions for voluntary pro-environmental choice (trustworthy gover-
nance, affordable sustainable alternatives, effective enforcement, and adequate consumer purchasing
power) are already in place. In low-and-middle-income countries, these preconditions are often absent
or uneven; and applying voluntary SCB frameworks here produces the very intention-behaviour gap that
dominates the literature, while misdiagnosing its cause. Drawing on scarcity cognition theory, common-
pool resource theory, and the institutional voids construct, the Institutional Precondition Threshold
Model is developed in this study, a two-axis framework that maps institutional quality against appropri-
ate SCB intervention type. The argument is that below an institutional threshold, enforcement-led in-
struments (source-level bans, deposit-return schemes, and upstream extended producer responsibility)
are the only viable first-order levers for circular consumption; voluntary frameworks regain predictive
validity only after that threshold is crossed.

detail.abstract: Energy system optimisation models increasingly inform low-carbon energy transition strategies, but conventional least-cost, central-planner formulations raise questions about who bears transition costs, whose perspectives shape scenarios, or which actors remain poorly represented. This paper examines how distributive, procedural and recognition justice enter-or fail to enter-TIMES-based modelling; what enables or constrains their treatment; and how pathway analysis could become more justiceresponsive. We conduct a theory-sensitising single-case study at VITO (Belgium) covering two models, TIMES-Be and TIB3R. As the TIMES framework is widely used for whole energy system planning, this policy-facing case exposes broader tensions between aggregate system efficiency and plural justice claims. Eight semi-structured interviews with experienced modellers were analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic approach. Findings indicate that justice rarely served as an explicit organising principle. Instead, it entered tacitly and unevenly through scenario framing, discounting, constraints, stakeholder engagement and post-processing. Aggregate affordability and acceptability were emphasised over analysis of differentiated costs and spatial burdens; industry actors had greater influence than households or the public; and heterogeneous household capacities and motivations so far remained weakly represented. These patterns arose from interactions among TIMES architecture, organisational conditions and modeller agency. Conceptually, the study relocates justice from a possible model add-on to a concern spanning the modelling lifecycle. For practice, it supports treating least cost as a reference rather than as a definition of fairness, combining TIMES with near-optimal, multi-criteria, behavioural, spatial and financial analyses, and strengthening participation and responsible transparency. Although not representative of the TIMES community, the case identifies testable propositions for comparative research across organisations and modelling traditions.

detail.abstract: When a public body answers an information request by saying it holds nothing responsive, the answer can take two evidentiary forms. It can be an attestation: a statement by a responsible official, offered in good faith, that a search was made and found nothing. Or it can be a record: a contemporaneous, reviewable account of what was searched, how, by whom and with what result. Freedom of information systems have developed the first form far more than the second. This article examines the consequences of that choice through doctrinal and comparative analysis of Brazil's Access to Information Law (Law 12,527/2011) and the administrative practice of the Mixed Commission for Reassessment of Information (CMRI), United States FOIA litigation, where agency declarations are the ordinary vehicle of proof, and United Kingdom tribunal practice. It advances three propositions. An attestation is a testimonial artefact: it is produced when review is anticipated, it is carried by a declarant who may not have performed the search, and it is consumed once. A search record is a documentary artefact that can be inspected, sampled and reused. And the difference matters beyond the single dispute, because negative answers are inputs to later institutional filters, which treat an untested attestation and a verifiable record identically. The article proposes a minimum content, custody and review-access rule for search records, to be implemented first through CMRI and CGU practice and archival regulation. The contribution is doctrinal, comparative and normative; the downstream hypothesis is untested and no empirical estimate is offered.
