detail.abstract: We ask whether the empirical evidence for rough volatility from daily spot returns is statistically identifying. Using the deterministic Wiener-chaos likelihood of Javaheri (2026) together with the (trivially) deterministic likelihood of the Guyon-Lekeufack 4-factor Markovian path-dependent volatility model, we run two conceptually distinct experiments on a common footing. First, a Vuong non-nested model-selection test confirms that when either model is the true data-generating process, the likelihood machinery correctly identifies it: in our simulation study 125 of 125 paths were correctly classified (75 of 75 under rBergomi truth and 50 of 50 under 4FMPDV truth). Second, and separately, we apply the rBergomi likelihood to synthetic data from the Guyon-Lekeufack SPX-calibrated smooth-Markovian process: it returns a median H = 0.115, essentially matching the empirical SPX value and below what Guyon and Lekeufack themselves report from the scaling estimator. The two results speak to different statistical questions. The first is a model-selection statement; the second is an identifiability statement. It is the identifiability result, rather than the modelselection result, that bears on the interpretation of the empirical literature, which reports H as evidence for fractional memory. Rough volatility remains a viable modeling choice-and separate theoretical arguments from option-market arbitrage give strong grounds to believe it holds-but the statistical evidence from daily SPX returns alone is less identifying than empirical estimates of H alone might suggest.

detail.abstract: Recent empirical work has documented a persistent gap between historical and optionimplied Hurst estimates for SPX volatility, typically interpreted as a nonzero-maturity smoothing bias of the estimator. We reinterpret the gap as a formal specification signal. Building on the paper-1 deterministic likelihood filter for rough Bergomi and the paper-2 identification failure under path-dependent volatility, we develop a measure-invariance framework in which the pathwise Hölder exponent H and, in the Guyon-Lekeufack class, the entire diffusion parameter vector, are Girsanov-invariant. The framework yields an asymmetric falsifiability result: rough Bergomi retains a level parameter ξ 0 that absorbs the variance risk premium, while Guyon-Lekeufack 4F PDV structurally cannot-and is therefore provably misspecified as a joint (P, Q) description in any market with nontrivial VRP. We construct a joint deterministic likelihood combining the WCE spot-return filter with a Q-side observation channel from either the multi-maturity ARS zero-vanna estimator (for option-chain data) or the CBOE VIX and SKEW pair at 30 days (for public data), together with a two-stage diagnostic architecture: model-class selection via surface residual, withinclass specification via Wald test on the measure-invariant subvector. Monte Carlo experiments confirm essentially perfect model-class identification at N = 10 3 trading days. We apply the diagnostic to SPX over 1990-2026 using CBOE public data, segmenting by VVIX-quantile regimes and rate-hike-cycle windows. The framework yields an economically interpretable regime-conditional outcome rather than a straightforward model selection: ĤP ≈ 0.11 across regimes matches the paper-2 attractor value consistently, while ĤQ separates from ĤP under low-VVIX calm and median conditions (W ≥ 7.5, reject at 5%) but agrees under high-VVIX stress, all three rate-hike cycles, and both the 2008 and 2020 crisis episodes. The pattern is consistent with the variance-risk-premium literature-the discrepancy emerges in regimes where the proportional VRP is documented to be largest-though we do not claim to establish a mechanistic mapping between VRP magnitude and the observed H-gap. GL is preferred by AIC in every regime slice on the Q side but faces the no-VRP obstruction of Theorem 1 against being a single-parameter-vector joint (P, Q) specification.

detail.abstract: Access to information statutes are usually examined through their exemptions, yet a considerable class of unsatisfied requests ends not in a refusal but in a declaration that the requested record does not exist or could not be located. Such a declaration is a factual negative whose only evidentiary basis lies with the authority that issues it. This article asks when, and on what record, the law should treat that negative as sufficient. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, it examines the Brazilian framework (Constitution arts. 5(XXXIII), 37 and 216(2); Law 12,527/2011; Law 8,159/1991; the Code of Civil Procedure), the interpretive practice of the Mixed Commission for Reassessment of Information (CMRI), notably Súmula 6/2015 and a purposive set of its decisions, and three external reference points: United States FOIA search-adequacy case law, United Kingdom tribunal practice on whether information is "held," and inter-American and European human-rights jurisprudence. The article advances two propositions. First, a bare declaration of non-existence is legally under-determined, because it is compatible with at least five distinct states of the world governed by different legal regimes. Second, the declaration does not stay where it is issued: under a working concept of cascade selectivity, later institutional filters treat the resulting absence as evidence of irrelevance. Brazilian practice, which treats the declaration as a satisfactory response and presumes its veracity, leaves a review gap between admissibility and verification. The article proposes a graduated, reviewable search-record standard that can be implemented largely through regulation and the CMRI's own interpretive practice. The contribution is doctrinal, comparative and normative; no empirical estimate is offered. detail.abstract: The five largest US cloud and AI infrastructure operators spent USD 448B on capital expenditure in 2025 and have guided to roughly USD 780B for 2026. Whether that capital earns its carry is not a question about the size of AI demand today but about how fast it must grow. We build a vintage model: capex cohorts from 2023, net of the 2022 pre-AI baseline, each split into silicon (economic life ~4 yr) and shell (life ~20 yr) with an energization lag, and compute the annual carry — depreciation, facility opex, and return on net book — for each year 2027–2030. The carry ramps from ~USD 390B in 2027 to ~USD 725B in 2030 if capex merely plateaus, because the 2025–27 cohorts are still on the books as new ones arrive. Against calendar-2026 AI revenue of USD 187B — decomposed into seven sourced components with a P10–P90 of USD 165–190B — we solve for the sustained growth rate at which the installed base breaks even: about 48%/yr through 2030 on a capex plateau, 62% under an arms race, 33% under a 35% capex cut. No plausible rate clears 2027–28; those years are a sunk deficit of USD 100–250B/yr. A second, independent estimate — fifteen sector Fermi chains, each with a 2026 base, a 2030 ceiling set by payroll, IT-budget or unit constraints, a ramp rate, and a cloud-capture share — delivers end-customer revenue of ~USD 625B in 2030 (P10–P90 USD 525–745B) with growth decaying from ~57% in 2027 to ~14% in 2030. Cloud receipts from those sectors are ~USD 490B against a 2030 carry of ~USD 725B: a deficit of USD 255B/yr, 3.5 standard deviations of the propagated uncertainty, and USD 190–540B/yr under an arms race. Nineteen inputs that carried most of the variance are each decomposed into sourced components, cutting the top-down root-sum-square from 286 to 104 and leaving the residual in two axes: an adoption/capability factor and the assistant ceiling. Over those two we map the probability that receipts exceed carry inside a feasibility band derived from Gartner enterprise software and services budgets. On a capex plateau the 50% contour requires 2030 AI revenue of ~USD 950B, requiring AI to take ~15% of all enterprise software and services spending by 2030; on a 35% capex cut the probability of profit reaches ~50% in 2030 and ~95% by 2032. Five structural mechanisms — slack absorption, verification, value leakage to integrators and on-device silicon, sovereignty carve-outs, and grid queues — set those ceilings. If the ceilings are wrong by a factor of 1.5, the build-out pays. The paper is a probability assessment, not a forecast: at the register's current inputs the most likely outcome is the deficit above, and that most likely outcome is overturned if calendar-2028 AI revenue exceeds USD 400B. Two reviewer points sharpen the supply side: if an accelerator's value tracks the marginal cost of inference on the newest chip, the silicon bought through 2026 is already worth USD 100–250B less than straight-line books imply; and if token prices converge on the marginal cash cost of inference, receipts converge on the opex line and the carry is never recovered. Goldman Sachs's September 2026 ROIC framework, restated per dollar of capital, requires 27 cents of annual revenue per dollar against the paper's 28; the two differ on scope and on one input, facility operating cost. Model, data and code are open and driven from a register of inputs; every input is appraised in an appendix, with an update protocol and a glossary. Version 27, 15 October 2026. detail.abstract: Equitable renewable-energy planning requires distinguishing abundant energy resources from actual access to infrastructure. This paper evaluates how modeled relative wealth, transmission-line proximity, road proximity, and longterm photovoltaic (PV) resource potential are geographically associated across Ghanaian settlements. The 2025 World Bank Distributed Renewable Energy Atlas provides 25,342 settlement records; 21,582 observations enter the principal complete-case analyses, and 21,576 enter the common-sample district-boundary comparison. Settlements in the lowest observed wealth quintile have a median distance of 13.1 km to an existing transmission line, versus 5.4 km in the highest quintile. Transmission-line and road-distance coefficients remain negative across region and district fixedeffects models under spatial heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent inference. In contrast, the solarpotential association varies substantially with geographic controls and spatial bandwidth. Residual spatial autocorrelation persists and missing wealth values are concentrated among smaller and more geographically remote settlements. The paper therefore documents a robust descriptive geography of infrastructure proximity but does not identify causal effects, verified electrification, or investment outcomes. Its policy contribution is an empirically cautious argument for screening decentralized-energy opportunities together with social vulnerability and measurement uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Throughout history, gold has been a highly valued investment, especially in times of crisis. In recent years, however, silver has attracted the attention of investors for its performance in terms of returns and price. Therefore, the objective of this research was to determine which of the two metals is the best to invest in. In this sense, an empirical method was developed based on the most common tests found in the literature, which included a financial integration with macroeconomic variables of the United States; predictability and trend analysis; return loss rate; volatility analysis; and annual returns. A quantitative research approach limited to the United States of America was established. The variables mainly used were the prices of gold and silver and their returns between 1990 and 2024. The statistical methods used in these tests were: Multiple Linear Correlation; Cubic ARIMA, GARCH and Polynomial Regression; Defects per Million Opportunities (DPMO); Bonett test for Difference of Variances; and Short, Medium and Long Term Returns Analysis. In order to synthesize and compare the results of the tests, an evaluation method based on the Pugh Matrix was used. As a result, gold received a score of +1, while silver got a value of-1, reaching the conclusion that of the two metals, gold is the best to invest in. Some findings and considerations are mentioned at the end.

detail.abstract: We explore the theoretical effects of government subsidies for carbon sequestration embodied in the current U.S. policy regime, showing the extent to which they induce firms to deploy costly technology for minimal net emission reductions. We model a representative firm producing a single output with two inputs of differing carbon intensity, and the ability to sequester a portion of its emissions subject to large fixed costs and increasing marginal capture costs. Our theoretical and numerical results show that firms induced to sequester under a carbon tax would also sequester under an equal-sized sequestration subsidy, but that the subsidy can induce adoption at much lower policy values due to captured emissions generating revenue that offsets fixed costs. We document the potential for economic distortions: unlike a carbon tax, sequestration credits do not encourage substitution toward less carbon-intensive inputs, and may instead incentivize firms to maintain or even shift production toward more carbon-intensive facilities in order to maximize credit revenue. Since capture is imperfect, this can increase uncaptured emissions even as sequestration rises.

detail.abstract: Today and throughout history, two activities use much of the world’s resources and effort: competition and conflict. Conflict as a strategic interaction amongst rational agents is of interest to game theory. At the same time, whether interstate or intrastate, conflict is an activity which consumes resources and affects total production. This twofold relation between conflict and economics connects my three essays on the Political Economy of Conflict and Growth. The first essay, Economic Growth and Defense Spending in the U.S, explores the economic effects of defense spending in the United States. The time series paper shows that different components of defense expenditure have different economic effects. In other words, the growth effects of defense outlays differ by type. Its effects are negative for some outlays, and positive for others. In single country studies, the paper’s result cautions against aggregating across different categories of military expenditures. The results are also applicable to cross sectional empirical work. My second essay, Generic Stability of Economic Equilibria, is theoretical. Using singularity theory, this paper explores the generic properties of Nash, Walrasian, ix and other economic equilibria. The results show that for any game among finite number of players with differentiable utility functions, Nash equilibria and Walrasian market equilibria are isolated points. The paper examines the effects of equity based refinements like envy free points and egalitarian equivalence. The results show that there are special examples where equilibria exist but not generically. The results of this paper are applicable to the effects of strong dependence amongst market agents, and sensitivity of economic equilibria to assumed functional forms. The results of this paper extend to shed light on the complexity of computation as well as standard game theoretic and competitive equilibria. My third essay, The Dynamics of Power in Political Systems, is a dynamic synthesis of static political-economic analysis of power relations among the people, the ruler, and the elite. After deriving more general sufficient conditions, the essay assumes these, now generalized, results of other papers in the literature that people’s need for security empowers the elite and the ruler and that the self-interested elite and ruler will not allow a weak population to regain any power. The essay consolidates the literature of political economy while providing a global perspective. The results show a global attractor wherein only the ruler and the elite share power. The paper also relaxes these assumptions and finds different local and global equilibria, but implies no stable interior equilibrium wherein all three: people power and elite share power.

detail.abstract: Understanding how households adapt to rising temperatures is central to evaluating the economic costs of climate change, yet evidence on adaptation in how households adapt remains limited. This paper studies behavioral adaptation in household food-at-home spending to temperature change by distinguishing short-run responses to weather fluctuations from long-run responses to persistent warming in the United States. Using household-level grocery transaction data matched with highresolution temperature records, we decompose realized temperature into a slow-moving climate norm and a short-run weather deviation, and we measure adaptation as the difference between the response to weather and the response to climate. We estimate behavioral responses on both the extensive margin, the decision to shop, and the intensive margin, expenditure conditional on shopping. We find that food-at-home spending declines with higher temperatures in both short and long-run, but the long-run climate response is much larger. A 1℃ increase in weekly temperature above the norm lowers expected weekly spending by about 0.5% (12.5 cents) per capita, while a 1℃ increase in the climate norm lowers weekly spending by about 1.9% (50 cents). Both effects and the difference between them are statistically significant. This implies that behavioral adaptation intensifies the short-run effect of heat. Responses vary across income groups, regions, and food categories, and differ between cold and heat exposure. These results highlight the importance of household purchase behavior for accurately measuring economic impact of climate change and the role of behavioral adaptation in adjusting long-run response to it.

detail.abstract: We develop a multiperiod model of the EU Emissions Trading System with two features: the probability of political collapse rises endogenously with the allowance price, and counterfactual emissions and the backstop price decline with technological progress. Despite the nonlinearity they introduce, the equilibrium price admits a closed form. Political risk deflates the leverage of the emissions cap and its decline rate, leaves bank side reserve operations nearly neutral, and activates technology, a lever powerless under full credibility. Calibrated to the 2026 EU ETS, observed prices and bank drawdowns jointly bound priced collapse risk near zero: a credibility puzzle the model maps.

detail.abstract: The deployment of clean technologies in hard-to-abate sectors is often hindered by high costs and investment risks. Carbon Contracts for Difference (CCfDs) have emerged to mitigate these risks, yet their design raises a central question: should support for competing clean technologies be technology-neutral or technology-specific? We study this question in a setting with two substitutable abatement technologies subject to technology-specific wedges between private and social costs, as well as cost shocks observed by firms but not by the regulator when policy is set. We compare uniform and technology-specific versions of price and quantity instruments. In a quadratic model, technology neutrality distorts the allocation whenever private--social cost wedges differ across technologies, while a neutral quota allows firms to reallocate deployment in response to realized relative costs. A common quota combined with technology-specific subsidies corrects the wedges while preserving this flexibility and therefore outperforms separate technology-specific quotas. The welfare gain from discrimination increases with substitutability between technologies. We micro-found aggregate costs using a distribution of heterogeneous production sites and apply the model to green and blue hydrogen in Europe. In this setting, the value of discrimination depends on the mass of sites near the adoption and technology-choice frontiers. Numerical simulations confirm that targeted support can generate substantial welfare gains. They show that, beyond the quadratic benchmark, the gains from discrimination may differ between price and quantity instruments because prices allow cost shocks to affect total deployment. These results highlight the value of combining technology-neutral competition with targeted corrections of technology-specific market failures.

detail.abstract: We study the joint prediction of the continuous future values of two widely used technical indicators-the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) and the Stochastic Oscillator-across 15 simultaneous horizons (h= 1 to 15, i.e., 5 to 75 minutes ahead) on 15 heterogeneous assets (forex, cryptocurrencies, equities) using 5-minute intraday data from 2010-2025 (53.7M raw rows; 4.0M after quality filtering). Predicting indicator values directly, rather than binary signals or raw prices, is operationally motivated: systematic trading systems consume indicator values as inputs to signal generators, EMA-based indicators give smoother regression targets than raw returns, and bounded oscillators such as the Stochastic avoid the non-stationarity of raw prices. To our knowledge, this continuous multi-output multi-horizon formulation across heterogeneous assets has not been explicitly addressed in prior work, which mostly targets binary signals or single-asset, single-horizon settings. Our contributions are: (i) a comparison of 12 architectures, from ARIMA and Ridge to XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Bi-LSTM, GRU, TCN, and TFT; (ii) per-asset target normalization and a learned ticker embedding, associated with a 2.8× increase in MACD Pearson correlation over a global LSTM baseline (0.265 to 0.753); (iii) an ablation study across three axes; and (iv) walk-forward validation over three non-overlapping windows suggesting stable behavior of GRU v3 (std ≈ 0.004). The GRU+TFT ensemble reaches 64.3%/63.5% Directional Accuracy (val/test) on MACD, versus 0% for the persistence baseline, which has higher Pearson correlation (0.773 vs. 0.718) but never predicts a directional change. For the Stochastic Oscillator, DA reaches 69.9%/69.8% (val/test), consistent across all evaluated learned models.

detail.abstract: Team formulation (TF) involves facilitating a group of professionals to build a holistic picture of a case and to develop a shared understanding of current difficulties and a forward care plan. SAFE, a service supporting victims and witnesses of crime, invites professionals to an online multi-agency meeting to engage in TF when a referral is received. This study uses one-to-one semi-structured interviews to explore professionals’ experiences of TF in these meetings. The findings highlight that professionals’ experiences were characterised by both emotional and practical challenges, alongside productive and reassuring aspects. The findings also outline several key elements that shaped the formulation process, including information sharing, collaborative planning, relationship building, and ongoing updates. Finally, the findings illustrate the facilitators’ contributions to the formulation process, particularly in establishing a sense of professional equity and applying expert knowledge. These findings support TF, however future research may benefit from evaluating the longer-term impacts of multi-agency TF delivered via videoconferencing. Findings from this study may help inform the development of outcome measures capable of supporting such research.
